investment_summary: TSMC's 2025 results show strong momentum. Revenue rose 31.6% to NT$3,809,054 million and net income 46.5% to NT$1,697,604 million, with gross margin at 59.9%, driven by HPC, now 58% of revenue [1]. Free cash flow of NT$992,378 million covered dividends about twice, and net cash reached NT$3.03 trillion by September 2026 [1][2].\n\nValuation is the open question. The shares trade on 18.6 times FY2026 consensus EPS [3]. The reverse DCF implies 23.6% annual revenue growth for ten years. That is above the 18.9% three-year historical CAGR, but far below consensus growth of 46.6% for FY2026 and 37.9% for FY2027 [2][3]. The price therefore needs growth above history for a decade, even though consensus expects much faster growth in the next two years. The implied 11.1% return barely exceeds the 11.0% cost of capital [2]. The main risks are customer concentration, export controls and the US$52–56 billion 2026 capex plan [1].
key_takeaways: AI-led HPC demand should keep margins near 60%, since gross margin rose to 59.9% and HPC is now 58% of revenue [1].
Self-funded expansion looks durable: free cash flow of NT$992 billion covered dividends about twice, leaving net cash of NT$2.06 trillion [1][2].
Rising estimates support the 18.6x forward P/E, but the implied return of about 11% only matches the cost of capital [2][3].
Customer concentration is the main risk: the ten largest customers took 78% of 2025 revenue, so one large customer's slowdown would hit results [1].
business_overview:
Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company, founded in 1987, is a dedicated foundry that manufactures chips to customers' proprietary designs, and it also offers design support, mask making, TSMC 3DFabric advanced stacking and packaging, and testing services [1]. Annual capacity exceeded 17 million 12-inch equivalent wafers in 2025, and shipments rose 16.3% to 15.0 million from 12.9 million in 2024 [1]. The company presents scale in advanced technologies as its main competitive advantage. The model is capital-intensive: because most capacity is owned, a large share of operating costs is fixed [1]. The filing gives no separate revenue for packaging and testing, which make up about 14% of net revenue, so their growth cannot be isolated [1].

Advanced nodes are the main differentiator. Technologies at 7 nanometers and below made up 74% of 2025 wafer revenue, up from 69% in 2024, and 3-nanometer rose to 24% of wafer revenue from 18% [1]. The 2-nanometer technology entered volume production during the year [1]. High Performance Computing became the largest platform at 58% of net revenue, up from 51%, with revenue of NT$2,192,931 million, up 48% [1]. Smartphone revenue grew 11% to NT$1,110,816 million, but its share fell to 29% from 35%. IoT and automotive each held 5% of net revenue, and digital consumer electronics 1% [1]. AI and server demand now sets the pace of the business more than handsets do.

Strategic initiatives centre on capacity outside Taiwan and on next-generation nodes. The 16-angstrom technology is expected in risk production in 2026, and the N3A automotive process was released at the end of 2025 [1]. TSMC Arizona entered high-volume production at the end of 2024, and a second facility is under construction, supported by direct CHIPS Act funding of up to US$6.6 billion [1]. JASM in Japan began volume production in December 2024, and ESMC in Dresden, 70% owned by the company, is the European project [1]. Carbon fees from 2026 and rising utility prices are the listed cost pressures [1]. Capital expenditure guidance for 2026 is US$52–56 billion, against NT$1,272,411 million spent in 2025 [1].
market_position:
Revenue is concentrated by customer headquarters: North America accounted for 75% of 2025 net revenue, Asia Pacific 9%, China 9%, Japan 4% and EMEA 3% [1]. The filing describes customers as many of the world's leading semiconductor companies, from fabless designers to integrated device manufacturers, but does not name them [1]. Customer concentration is the key feature: the ten largest customers accounted for 78% of 2025 net revenue, up from 70% in 2023, and the largest single customer for 19%, down from 25% in 2023 [1].

The filing gives no market share figure and describes the company only as a leader of the foundry segment [1]. Its position rests on advanced-node scale and on the packaging capability that AI accelerators need, with CoWoS and SoIC named as HPC drivers [1]. The main competitive threat is large customers designing their own chips and working directly with foundries, which the filing says could cause significant variation in sales if AI demand proves volatile [1].

Market sentiment is strongly positive. The 52-week share price range was US$143.33 to US$387.17 [2]. The consensus rating is Buy, with a mean target price of US$586.69 in a range of US$440 to US$1,000 [3]. Those analyst figures were retrieved on 25 November 2026, after the filing, and reflect opinion rather than the filing itself. The consensus forward P/E of 18.6 times is the relevant valuation anchor [3].
operating_results:
Net revenue rose 31.6% to NT$3,809,054 million in 2025, led by wafer shipments up 16.3% and by advanced nodes at 74% of wafer revenue [1]. Cost of revenue grew 20.3%, slower than revenue, so gross margin rose to 59.9% from 56.1% and gross profit reached NT$2,281,294 million, despite a stronger NT dollar [1]. Operating margin widened to 50.8% from 45.7%, and net income attributable to shareholders rose 46.5% to NT$1,697,604 million, a net margin of 44.6% against 40.0% [1]. Diluted EPS reached NT$327.35, up from NT$226.25 [1].

Currency was the main headwind. The NT dollar strengthened from NT$32.13 to NT$31.11 per US dollar, reducing reported revenue, and the filing puts each 1% depreciation of the US dollar at roughly 0.3 percentage points of operating margin [1]. R&D rose 20.7% to NT$246,427 million for 10-, 14- and 16-angstrom work, and income tax expense rose 39.6% to NT$346,530 million, an effective rate of about 17.0% [1]. Operating cash flow reached NT$2,274,976 million and capital expenditure NT$1,272,411 million, leaving free cash flow of NT$992,378 million, which covered dividends of NT$466,779 million about twice [1].

Consensus expects growth to continue. FY2026 revenue is estimated at about NT$5.58 trillion (+46.6%) and FY2027 at about NT$7.70 trillion (+37.9%), with EPS of US$17.50 and US$23.39 per ADR [3]. The data source labels these revenue figures in dollars, but the growth rates reconcile with the NT$ base reported in the filing, so they are shown in NT$ here. These figures were retrieved on 25 November 2026, after the filing. Estimates have risen: FY2026 EPS is up 4.8% over 90 days and FY2027 EPS 9.9%, and TSMC beat quarterly EPS consensus in each of the last four quarters, by 1.7% to 10.9% [3]. Net cash reached NT$3.03 trillion and trailing free cash flow NT$1.46 trillion at 30 September 2026 [2].
risk_assessment:
The largest risk is customer concentration in a cyclical end market. The ten largest customers accounted for 70%, 76% and 78% of net revenue in 2023, 2024 and 2025, and the filing links this to the structural shift toward HPC and smartphone applications [1]. Because most manufacturing capacity is owned, a large share of operating costs is fixed and does not fall when utilization drops [1]. A loss or curtailment of a top customer therefore hits margins as well as revenue. The filing also notes that customers designing their own chips could cause significant swings in sales if AI demand proves volatile [1]. It offers no backlog or long-term contract data to offset this exposure [1].

Trade and export-control exposure is the second risk. The majority of principal production facilities and revenue sit in the R.O.C., while the company sells globally into a regulatory environment that changed several times in the past two years [1]. The filing lists the April 2025 baseline tariff, reciprocal tariffs from August 2025, a February 2026 court ruling against IEEPA-based tariffs, and a 25% Section 232 tariff on certain advanced computing chips announced in December 2025, and says the effects are still unclear [1]. The Nanjing fab now operates under an annual export license with no assurance of renewal [1]. Government incentives reduce some cost exposure but carry conditions on where the company can expand, and noncompliance could lead to repayment [1].

Physical disruption is the third risk. The company recorded net earthquake losses of about NT$3 billion in the second quarter of 2024 and NT$5.3 billion in the first quarter of 2025, after insurance [1]. The filing also flags power shortages, water rationing and recurring utility price increases, along with sole-sourced inputs and a limited equipment supplier base [1]. The three risks connect: a disruption at a single site hits the same customers who already account for most revenue. The financial buffers are strong, though. The Altman Z-Score is 15.77, the Piotroski F-Score 9 of 9 and the Beneish M-Score -2.70, below the manipulation warning threshold [2]. The main funding test is the 2026 capex plan of US$52–56 billion, which would strain operating cash flow if it does not keep pace [1].
competitors_analysis:
Three US-listed peers were chosen from the candidate list. UMC is a pure-play wafer foundry and the closest match to TSMC's business model. ASE Technology (ASX) provides packaging and testing that overlaps with TSMC's advanced packaging, and is the closest in size among the candidates, at about 0.2 times TSMC's revenue [4]. GlobalFoundries (GFS) is a US-listed pure-play foundry, though it focuses on mainstream nodes. Intel was excluded because it is an integrated device maker rather than a foundry [4].

TSMC leads the group on profitability. Its 2025 gross margin of 59.9% compares with 29.0% at UMC, 24.9% at GFS and 17.7% at ASX [4]. Revenue growth of 31.6% compares with 8.4% at ASX, 2.3% at UMC and 0.6% at GFS, and ROIC of 26.7% compares with 9.9% at UMC, 7.9% at ASX and 7.2% at GFS [4]. Peer revenue in 2025 was below 2022 levels at all three, while TSMC's 2025 revenue was well above its 2022 level [4]. EBITDA margins fell at each peer over 2022 to 2025, while TSMC's rose slightly to 72.0% [4]. Free cash flow conversion is not compared, because the source does not define the ratio and its values cannot be reproduced from the table [4].

The premium valuation tracks the operating gap. TSMC's trailing EV/EBITDA rose from 7.2 in 2022 to 17.3 in 2025, the highest in the peer set, against a 2025 peer median of about 8.5 [2][4]. EBITDA grew 72.1% over the period while the multiple more than doubled, so most of the rerating reflects a higher price for the same earnings stream rather than a large margin shift [4]. On forward figures, consensus puts TSMC at 18.6 times FY2026 EPS [3]. The peer data does not disclose the drivers of TSMC's growth, so the durability of this premium cannot be verified from these figures alone [4].

investment_theses.thesis: Advanced-node and HPC mix keeps gross margin near 60% through 2026, so margin is not a cyclical casualty of the capex cycle.
investment_theses.evidence: Gross margin rose to 59.9% from 56.1%; 7nm-and-below reached 74% of wafer revenue and HPC 58% of net revenue [1].
investment_theses.signpost: Reported quarterly gross margin at or above 58% in each 2026 quarter, confirmed in Q4 2026 results (early 2027).
investment_theses.invalidation: Gross margin falling back to the 2024 level of 56.1% or below, or 7nm-and-below share of wafer revenue declining in a filing [1].

investment_theses.thesis: Operating cash flow can fund the 2026 capex plan without a rise in debt, so the balance sheet stays net-cash.
investment_theses.evidence: 2025 free cash flow was NT$992,378 million against capex of NT$1,272,411 million; net cash was NT$3.03 trillion at 30 September 2026, with trailing free cash flow of NT$1.46 trillion [1][2].
investment_theses.signpost: Trailing free cash flow above about NT$1.3 trillion, matching 2025 capex, in the Q4 2026 filing (early 2027), with total debt flat near NT$1.06 trillion.
investment_theses.invalidation: Total debt rising materially to fund capex or dividends, or net cash falling below NT$2 trillion [1][2].

investment_theses.thesis: Consensus earnings revisions keep rising, so the stock can grow into its forward multiple rather than rely only on rerating.
investment_theses.evidence: FY2026 EPS consensus is up 4.8% and FY2027 up 9.9% over 90 days, with TSMC beating quarterly EPS in each of the last four quarters by 1.7% to 10.9% [3].
investment_theses.signpost: FY2027 EPS consensus holding at or above US$23 and at least one more quarterly EPS beat in the Q4 2026 results (early 2027).
investment_theses.invalidation: A quarterly EPS miss, or more estimate cuts than raises over 30 days, which would show the growth path is slipping [3].
